newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer - no EMU special case for German unity.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer - no EMU special case for German unity.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Tuesday the costs of German reunification could be taken into account in deciding if it qualified for EMU, but that no special case could be expected.

Tietmeyer said that, while Germany could not expect a special reunification bonus in deciding if it met the criteria, if reunification were to be considered, then it would take into account the criteria regarding government debt. Government debt is one of the strict deficit, national debt and inflation criteria on EMU entry laid out in the Maastricht Treaty.
Tietmeyer said in the Wednesday edition of the Neue Westfaelische newspaper that Germany had been forced to take over the lion's share of debt from the former East Germany.
"That should be taken into account when deciding on whether Germany qualifies for EMU," said Tietmeyer.

Tietmeyer's comments come on the day when Germany's top economic institutes said Bonn has a chance to make a "point landing" on its budget deficit to qualify for EMU, but urged quick action to reform and consolidate state finances.

The institutes said Bonn's outstanding debt is likely to exceed the 60 percent of GDP, but it will probably plead that the costs of German unification are a "special factor" that should be taken into consideration, they said.

The Bundesbank President said that current prognoses about who will take part in European Economic and Monetary Union were invalid, as the candidates would be examined early next year to see who meets the Maastricht criteria for membership.
A stable currency union without Germany and France would not be possible, Tietmeyer said.

Tietmeyer went on to say that the criteria which specifies a government deficit of three percent of GDP was not chiefly about whether a country reached three percent, but a question of the sustainability of a country's economic situation.
However, the three percent criteria played an important role, and it was important for the common currency, the euro, that it be accepted and win trust.
